claims.text: Increasing Zr and Hf content in a boride-based component will improve its resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion.
Increasing Zr and Hf content promotes a more stable microstructure.
Increasing Zr and Hf content promotes protective oxide formation.
The Zr/Hf-enriched material forms a chemically homogeneous, single-phase hexagonal structure.
A chemically homogeneous, single-phase hexagonal structure has improved microstructural stability.
The homogeneous, stable structure promotes development of stable protective oxide layers.
Increasing Zr and Hf content increases the thermal-oxidative resistance of the high-entropy boride.
Increasing Zr and Hf content facilitates formation of stable compounds and protective oxide layers.
Stable compounds and protective oxide layers reduce molten-aluminum penetration and attack.
The Zr/Hf-enriched material has reduced porosity.
Porosity acts as an initiation site for molten-aluminum corrosion.
Relative to the conventional material, the Zr/Hf-enriched component will exhibit reduced mass loss during molten-aluminum exposure.
Relative to the conventional material, the Zr/Hf-enriched component will exhibit less surface degradation during molten-aluminum exposure.
Conventional compositions with lower Zr and Hf content have lower thermal-oxidative resistance.
Conventional boride-based components are more susceptible to molten-aluminum corrosion than Zr/Hf-enriched components.
The improvement remains effective only within a temperature and exposure-time range in which the high-entropy boride remains single-phase.
The supporting thermal-oxidative-resistance result was obtained in gas-dynamic tests rather than molten-aluminum exposure tests.
Oxidative and molten-metal environments may involve different corrosion mechanisms.
